worlds.name: The Ledger
worlds.summary: A quiet, exact brand that treats a finished project as a matter of record.
worlds.naming_direction: Words from record-keeping and proof: entries, receipts, ledgers, marks.

sample_names.name: Entry
sample_names.rationale: One word from the world of records; short enough to say in a group chat.

sample_names.name: Standing
sample_names.rationale: What a student builds over time, and what a teammate wants to know about.

worlds.tagline_direction: Flat statements of fact rather than promises — what happened, who confirmed it.
voice_rules: State the fact before the benefit.
Use numbers where a number exists, and nothing where it doesn't.
Never describe a person, only what they finished.
worlds.voice_sample_line: Four projects finished. Three teammates confirmed it. That's the whole profile.

typography.rationale: Monospace reads as a record rather than a pitch.
Neutral enough to disappear behind the facts.

imagery: Screenshots of the record itself, never stock photos of students laughing
Close crops of handwriting, stamps and signatures
composition: Left-aligned rows, generous line spacing, no centred hero text
Rules and dividers instead of cards and shadows
worlds.audience_perception: Serious and slightly institutional — reassuring to someone who has been let down, cold to someone looking for friends.
risks: Can feel like a credit score for people
Little warmth to attract students who have not yet been burned
opportunities: The only student brand that looks like evidence rather than marketing
Ages well: the record gets more valuable every term
obvious_ideas_rejected: A friendly campus-blue app with rounded corners — the default student-product look, so it disappears next to every other one.
A trust-badge and five-star world — the marketplace pattern, which turns classmates into ratings.
A hustle-culture world of late nights and grind — predictable for student builders and unrelated to reliability.

worlds.name: Crew Room
worlds.summary: The warm backstage of a theatre: people who have worked together and want to again.
worlds.naming_direction: Backstage and workshop language: crews, call sheets, green rooms, benches.

sample_names.name: Green Room
sample_names.rationale: Where the people who are about to make something wait together.

sample_names.name: Call Sheet
sample_names.rationale: A document that says exactly who is expected and when.

sample_names.name: The Bench
sample_names.rationale: Who you can call on, without implying a ranking.

worlds.tagline_direction: Spoken, slightly dry lines about turning up for each other.
voice_rules: Write the way a teammate texts, not the way a brand announces.
Admit the awkward part before offering the fix.
No exclamation marks; the warmth is in the words.
worlds.voice_sample_line: You already know who shows up. This is just somewhere to keep that written down.

typography.rationale: A warm serif with enough character to feel handmade.
Plain and friendly under an expressive heading.

imagery: Hands and workspaces mid-project, faces mostly out of frame
Pinned notes, whiteboards and half-finished builds
composition: Slightly off-grid placement, as though pinned up rather than laid out
Text over texture, with room left empty
worlds.audience_perception: Approachable and human — feels like a community, which may raise the question of whether it solves anything.
risks: Warmth can read as soft on the reliability problem
Theatre language may not land with engineering students
opportunities: Something students would mention to a friend unprompted
Makes confirming a teammate feel generous rather than judgemental
obvious_ideas_rejected: A campus social network in pastel gradients — the safe student-app look that dies without daily use.
A sports-team metaphor of drafts and line-ups — the obvious teamwork analogy, and it makes people into picks.
A productivity world of checklists and streaks — predictable for group work and faintly exhausting.

worlds.name: Plain Terms
worlds.summary: An editorial brand that says the uncomfortable thing out loud, in print-quality type.
worlds.naming_direction: Short declarative phrases from everyday speech about commitment.

sample_names.name: Who's In
sample_names.rationale: The actual question a student asks before a project starts.

sample_names.name: Said and Done
sample_names.rationale: Names the gap the product closes, in four syllables.

worlds.tagline_direction: Complete sentences that name the risk, with no hedging.
voice_rules: Say the uncomfortable thing in the first sentence.
One idea per sentence; no lists of benefits.
Never use a word a student wouldn't say out loud.
worlds.voice_sample_line: Half the people who promise to help won't. Find out before the deadline, not after.

typography.rationale: Tight, newspaper-grade sans that can be set very large.
Long-form serif that signals something worth reading.

imagery: Almost none — type does the work
Occasional documentary photography, black and white
composition: One enormous headline per screen, everything else small
Strict columns and a visible baseline grid
worlds.audience_perception: Grown-up and a little confrontational — credible, but it asks the reader to face something.
risks: Bluntness can read as pessimism about their classmates
Type-led design is unforgiving if the words are weak
opportunities: Nothing else in the category sounds like an editorial
The voice carries straight into launch copy without redesign
obvious_ideas_rejected: A reassuring "we've got you" world — the standard comfort brand, which quietly avoids naming the problem.
A tech-forward dark interface with charts — the default for anything involving a score.
A gamified world of badges and levels — predictable for students and trivialises being let down.
